content: The hepatitis A vaccine can be utilized for post-exposure prophylaxis across all populations and settings. This approach offers several public health benefits, including the induction of active immunity, which provides longer-lasting protection compared to immune globulin (IG). Additionally, the vaccine is easier to administer, more widely accepted, and readily available, with a cost per dose comparable to IG. The increased availability and ease of administration of the hepatitis A vaccine may also lead to a higher number of at-risk individuals receiving post-exposure prophylaxis. The risk of hepatitis A virus (HAV) transmission varies significantly depending on host and environmental factors, as well as the specific setting. For instance, in household settings without post-exposure prophylaxis, secondary attack rates of 15% to 30% have been reported. Transmission rates are higher when the infected individual is a young child compared to an adolescent or adult. Conversely, the attack rates among patrons of food service establishments exposed to HAV-infected food handlers are generally low. Most food handlers with hepatitis A do not transmit the virus to exposed consumers or restaurant patrons. Given the variability in HAV transmission risks across different settings, the magnitude of risk in each situation is a critical factor in deciding whether to use IG or the vaccine for post-exposure prophylaxis. Older individuals and those with chronic liver disease are more likely to experience severe manifestations of hepatitis A. Among older children and adults, infection is typically symptomatic, with jaundice occurring in over 70% of cases. Fulminant hepatitis has been reported more frequently in older patients with hepatitis A. Although individuals with chronic liver disease are not at increased risk of HAV infection, they are at higher risk for fulminant hepatitis A. Preventing hepatitis A in exposed older individuals and those with chronic liver disease is particularly important due to the frequency of severe outcomes. However, the efficacy of the hepatitis A vaccine as post-exposure prophylaxis in these groups has not been assessed in recent clinical trials and remains unknown. In contrast, IG has been successfully used for many years in these populations and the general population. The updated recommendations replace previous Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) guidelines for post-exposure prophylaxis with IG. They incorporate new recommendations for the use of single-antigen hepatitis A vaccine and updated guidance for IG use. These recommendations also consolidate existing guidelines regarding settings where post-exposure prophylaxis is indicated, such as close personal contact with an individual with hepatitis A or specific circumstances involving hepatitis A in a food handler or child care center. The updated recommendations maintain the guidance that post-exposure prophylaxis (using either the vaccine or IG) should be administered as soon as possible. There is no evidence regarding the efficacy of IG or the vaccine if administered more than two weeks after exposure. The updated recommendations for using the hepatitis A vaccine alone for post-exposure prophylaxis do not apply to the combination hepatitis A/hepatitis B vaccine, as no data exist on its performance for prophylaxis after HAV exposure. The concentration of HAV antigen in the currently available combination vaccine is half that of the single-antigen vaccine from the same manufacturer. Information on the relative efficacy of the vaccine compared to IG for post-exposure prophylaxis is limited, and no data are available for individuals over 40 years of age or those with underlying medical conditions. Therefore, decisions to use the vaccine or IG should consider patient characteristics associated with more severe manifestations of hepatitis A, such as older age and chronic liver disease. For healthy individuals aged 12 months to 40 years, the single-antigen hepatitis A vaccine at the age-appropriate dose is preferred over IG due to its advantages, including long-term protection and ease of administration.
